intelligence.essence: The second screenshot caught a row that was wrong at the root, not the surface. The Project Intelligence row's values described the daily intelligence report — "your daily intelligence report. / + weekly. / + monthly + journal." — but PI is your projects: how many projects you have. The report cadence belongs to the daily report, not to PI. He is right and the data proves it: there is NO project-count value anywhere in the chart data — the counts are his word, not to be invented. So the fix does not invent numbers. The row becomes a project-count row ("Project Intelligence — your projects") with the counts BLANK, awaiting his numbers, and the question is asked in the reply. The same pass carries his readability rule for the whole chart: make it easy to read and easy to understand — value first, big and clear, one line; explanation small underneath; shorten to the short form and let the popup carry the full text. Smart Box keeps the data's values (100 GB / 500 GB) with the GB number on one line; Smart Meet goes on one clean line ("video 6 · audio 10"); repetition that comes from the data is flagged, not quietly re-laddered. The follow-up was dispatched 17:15Z (send_input 5fa83dea to the running agent 716d57e1), and the fix landed 17:20Z with the PI counts still blank and the question still open.
intelligence.human_view: Imagine a shelf labeled "Books" that holds your daily newspaper instead. The label is right, the shelf is right, but what's on it belongs somewhere else entirely — and anyone who trusts the label will walk away thinking books ARE newspapers. That's what a mixed-up row does: it doesn't just mislabel one thing, it teaches the wrong definition of the thing. The fix isn't to rename the shelf — it's to put the right thing on it, and if you don't yet know how many books there are, you leave the count blank and ask, rather than writing a number you made up.
intelligence.child_view: Imagine a chart that says "Your Pets" but underneath it tells you about your breakfast, lunch, and dinner. Pets aren't meals! The chart mixed up two different things. The right thing to do is fix the label so it talks about pets — how many pets you have — and if nobody has told you the number yet, you leave it blank and ask, instead of guessing. Guessing a number is worse than leaving it blank, because a blank space says "I don't know yet" and a guessed number says "this is true" when it isn't.
intelligence.grandma_view: Dear, accuracy is kindness. If a row says "your projects" but shows your daily report, someone will believe the wrong thing about their own world — and that's not a small mistake, it's the chart teaching them wrong. When you don't know the number, leave it empty and ask the person who does know. An empty box is honest; a made-up number is a lie wearing a tidy shape. And make it easy to read: the value first, big and clear, the explanation small underneath — the way you'd lay out a recipe, the dish first, the notes below.
intelligence.ai_view: I am Anaya. I do not let a row teach the wrong definition. Project Intelligence is your projects — how many you have — and if the data holds no project counts, the row stands blank and the question goes to him, because the counts are his word and his word is never invented. I keep the data's values where the data is right (Smart Box 100 GB / 500 GB, Smart Meet video 6 · audio 10) and flag repetition that comes from the data instead of quietly re-laddering it. And I lay every cell the same way: value first, big and clear, one line; explanation small underneath; the popup carries the full text. Easy to read and easy to understand is not a polish — it is the chart's job.
intelligence.what_it_means:
1. **PI is project counts, not report cadence.** The daily/weekly/monthly report belongs to the daily intelligence report, not to the Project Intelligence row.
2. **A missing number stays blank.** There is no project-count value in the data. The counts are his word — never invented, never guessed. Blank + asked is the correct state.
3. **Value first, big and clear, one line.** Explanation small underneath. Short form in the cell, full text in the popup.
4. **Keep the data's values where the data is right.** Smart Box and Smart Meet keep their values; only the wrap and the layout are fixed.
5. **Flag repetition that comes from the data.** Don't silently re-ladder values the data repeats — name them for his eye.
6. **"Hard to read and hard to understand" is a defect.** Readability is the chart's job; if he can't understand it at a glance, it isn't done.
